The reason to tell this particular drift is not that the old meaning was true and the new one is false. It is that the new one arrived on a specific date, in specific company, doing a specific job — and a meaning with a birth certificate can be argued with in a way that a timeless fact cannot. The Weird Sisters were probably witches. See the wall above. The best scholarship on the question says Shakespeare wrote weyward and meant it, and that the Fates were put back into the play by an editor in 1733. Anyone reclaiming those three women as figures of fate is reclaiming Theobald’s text. It is still a good reclamation. It is not the one the First Folio supports. Nobody chooses to be read as weird. Weird Pride is a reclamation, and reclamations are for people who already carry the word whether they want it or not. The people who can put weirdness on and take it off again are not the ones the word costs anything. Weirdwashing is the failure mode: the aesthetic of deviance, adopted by an institution that will still send the same child out of the same room.

records.heading: Still taking shape
records.text:
Helen ends her essay by putting worth back where she found it: Specimen — the close The middle sister is the one holding the bucket. Not what has come to pass, and not what is owed — the one whose name is a verb still running. Verðandi: becoming. A life is not a point on a distribution. It is a thing being carved, in the present participle, and nobody has finished reading it yet. Find out more about Weird Pride, which falls on 4 March, and which Helen observes in July on the grounds that every day is one. Provenance
 Mounted 8 September 2026.
 Label corrected four times and re-determined once — the byline first, and on Helen Edgar’s own word.

quotes.text:
I think this is what wyrd actually means, human worth that was never about being static, never about being plotted somewhere along someone else’s bell curve, but about always moving, always still taking shape.

Let’s embrace our wyrd, weirdness, and everyone else’s too.
quotes.source: Helen Edgar, Wyrd, Weird, and the Invention of Normal, More Realms, July 2026.

records.text: This page is the working ledger, generated from ATTRIBUTIONS.md in the repository rather than retyped from it, so the copy you are reading cannot drift from the copy a session edits. Its risk is a wrong attribution, and the entries below are what a reader has instead of taking our word for it. The ledger for every quotation and credited idea on this site: what we quoted, whose it is, where it came from, and the day somebody read the primary and confirmed the wording. Why this file exists. Star Stuff keeps a FACTCHECK.md because its risk is a wrong fact. This site's risk is a wrong attribution — a definition trimmed to fit, an object generalized, a paraphrase left wearing somebody's name. Queering Earth re-reads other people's work, so nearly every page carries somebody else's words, and the citation is the only evidence a reader has. A search of our own library is not verification. See the credit-source skill. What that rule is aimed at, and what it is not (added 2026-09-08). It is aimed at our own prose — a glossary gloss, a summary, a paraphrase — being read back later as somebody else's wording. That is the Kelly-on-Eno scenius failure: the thing being confirmed was a rewrite, and five files agreeing with each other were one witness. It is not a rule that Ryan's quote collection is unusable. A direct quotation he transcribed from a paper he read, published with a citation to that paper, is a first-hand reading with the source named. Papers get rented, access lapses, and refusing to quote anything we cannot re-open today would discard years of legitimate collecting and quietly imply he did not read what he says he read. So: re-reading is an upgrade, not a precondition. Where the primary is reachable, read it and say which copy — that is how the Jack edition difference below was found. Where it is not, quote it with the citation attached and name whose transcription it is. The citation is the thing that has to be right.

records.heading: Verified
records.text: Octavia E. Butler — the Parable novels, and a preview that crossed a book boundary Quoted on: Other People Who Have It, Sheet No. 10. There are two Butlers on this site and they are not related. Judith Butler is credited below for a stylized repetition of acts. This entry is Octavia E. Butler, and every new entry for either has to carry the given name. Eight quotations, from two novels. All eight read from the Kindle editions Ryan holds, off the pages themselves — Readwise syncs highlights from the device rather than transcribing them, so the wording is the edition's wording and not a typist's. From Parable of the Sower: Those three and the "family business" paragraph are p. 11 and p. 12. The biological-conscience passage is p. 115, and the shared-pleasure passage runs pp. 265–266. From Parable of the Talents, all on p. 9: the "every damned bruise" paragraph, "They refused to let me be handicapped," and "So why do I miss it now?" THE TALENTS QUOTATIONS ARRIVED FILED AS SOWER, AT A PAGE NUMBER THAT WAS NOT A PAGE NUMBER, AND THAT IS THE ENTRY TO READ BEFORE CITING ANY EBOOK HERE. The Kindle file for Sower carries a publisher's preview of Talents after the novel ends and marks the join nowhere. Location 4758 is "decided to call this place Acorn," the last line of Sower; highlights run on to 5541. A Readwise export takes its title from the file, so highlights from two books arrive under one heading. The tell is a page counter that stops. The reader shows "Page 330 of 330" at 85% of the file, because the print-page map covers Sower only and then repeats its own last page. So the brief's Parable of the Sower (p. 330) was wrong twice: wrong book, and a number that was never a page. Re-titling alone would have been worse than leaving it — right book, plausible number, no relation to the text. The real page came off the standalone Talents, which reads 9 of 394 under its own running head. An appended preview is a second work inside one file, and every tool in the chain takes the file as the unit: page map, export title, highlight location. A citation is only as good as the assumption that one file is one book, and that assumption is quietly false at the end of most ebooks sold today. Sources: Octavia E. Butler, Parable of the Sower, Kindle edition, ASIN B008HALO4Q; and Parable of the Talents, Kindle edition, ASIN B008HALPHC. The PDF held in the Stimpunks Knowledge System at inbox/Butler, Octavia - Parable of the Sower.pdf is not a usable verification copy: it is missing chapters 9 and 21 of 25, and its em-dashes are OCR-damaged. Verified: 2026-09-10, from the reader's own pages. Sami Schalk — Bodyminds Reimagined, and two clauses that differ from the novel Quoted on: Other People Who Have It, Sheet No. 10. Seven quotations, read from the chapter PDFs held in SKS. Page numbers are the printed folios, each confirmed against the running head at the foot of its own page: the Introduction at p. 5; chapter 3 at pp. 89, 92, 95, 96, 100 and 111. The sheet leans hardest on this one, and quotes it whole because trimming it would make it a stronger claim than she made: Two clauses of the biological-conscience passage read differently where Schalk quotes it than in the edition read here, and both cite Sower 115: Butler, Kindle edition, p. 115 Schalk, Bodyminds Reimagined, p. 99 "They could kill if they had to" "They would kill if they had to" "But if everyone could feel everyone else's pain" "But if everyone else could feel everyone else's pain" A third, at Sower 12: the doctors call it an "organic delusional syndrome" in the novel and an "organic delusion syndrome" at Schalk p. 88. Unresolved, and it is an edition question rather than a doubt about either party. This site has twice found a real difference between printings where it expected a slip — Woolf's 1926 against her 1930, above, and Rossetti's colon. One piece of evidence cuts the other way and is recorded so nobody re-derives it: the pagination agrees. Both land the passage on p. 115, and a Kindle page map is keyed to a specific print setting, so two printings that agree on where p. 115 falls are likelier to be one setting than to differ in three words of it. Suggestive, not conclusive. The sheet quotes the novel, names its edition, and says on the page that Schalk's rendering differs. Neither disputed clause is one the argument rests on, and the sentence everything turns on — A biological conscience is better than no conscience at all — is identical in both. Settling it needs a 1993 or Seven Stories printing, which nobody here holds. Sources: Sami Schalk, Bodyminds Reimagined: (Dis)ability, Race, and Gender in Black Women's Speculative Fiction, Duke University Press, 2018. Chapter PDFs held in SKS at inbox/9780822371830-001.pdf (Introduction) and inbox/9780822371830-004.pdf (chapter 3). Verified: 2026-09-10. Stuart Murray and Susan Wendell are named on the sheet as Schalk cites them and are not quoted; Alison Kafer is her chapter epigraph and is not quoted here at all, because we have not read Feminist, Queer, Crip. Kimber, Verrier and Connolly — the empathy study, and the year everything convenient got wrong Quoted on: Other People Who Have It, Sheet No. 10. pp. 325, 325 and 326. Seventy-six Autistic participants. THE ISSUE YEAR IS 2024 AND EVERYTHING CONVENIENT SAYS 2023 — the DOI slug aut.2023.0001, and the repository deposit record for the accepted manuscript. Second instance of a pattern, after Experiences of autistic joy, where 2025 was the online-first date and the issue was 2026. Online-first year is not issue year, and a DOI slug is not a date. A paper newly cited on this site takes its volume, issue, pages and year from a bibliographic database, never from the PDF, the DOI, or a deposit record. Cite Mary Ann Liebert, not SAGE. Crossref returns SAGE because SAGE acquired the journal after publication; the article's own first page says Liebert. Name the imprint on the artefact, which is the reasoning that already makes a sheet name the printing it read. The accepted manuscript may not supply a word of the wording. Both states are held, and the accepted text is the authors' British-spelled pre-copy-edit copy. The differences are not all orthographic: the abstract's Conclusion is a different sentence, "but to better bridge the gap" against "but also better bridge the gap." Anybody assuming the two differed only in -ise and -ize would have quoted it wrong while feeling careful. And the version of record disagrees with itself on the headline figure, which is the detail a later hand is most likely to tidy: "Seventy-eight percent" in the Results at p. 325, "seventy eight percent" where the Discussion restates it at p. 326. The sheet quotes the Results occurrence. A sheet quoting both must reproduce both forms. The participants are quoted with no identifiers at all — no pseudonym, number or demographic tag. This ledger credits study participants by the names their paper gives them where there are any; here there are none, so the sheet's caption says the anonymity is the paper's and not our omission. Those two look identical on the page. Sources: Lesley Kimber, Diarmuid Verrier and Stephen Connolly, "Autistic People's Experience of Empathy and the Autistic Empathy Deficit Narrative," Autism in Adulthood 6, no. 3 (2024): 321–330, Mary Ann Liebert, Inc., doi:10.1089/aut.2023.0001. Version of record held in SKS at inbox/aut.2023.0001.pdf; accepted manuscript at inbox/Verrier-AutisticPeoplesExperience(AM).pdf. Verified: 2026-09-10, from the version of record, with the citation corroborated in Crossref and in the NLM's PubMed record, PMID 39371354 — two libraries that index independently of each other. David Gray-Hammond and Karla McLaren — Autistic hyper-empathy in the first person Quoted on: Other People Who Have It, Sheet No. 10. David Gray-Hammond, Hyper-empathy, mirror-touch synesthesia, and the Autistic experience of pain, 24 July 2023. Cited at neurohubcommunity.org, which is where he publishes now; the emergentdivergence.com address the SKS bookmark carries is his old domain, and Ryan confirmed the move. Karla McLaren, Autism, empathy, and the mind-blindness of everyday people. The emphasis on lack and surplus is hers. This is the quotation the sheet is named for: Lauren Olamina writes "I wish I could find other people who have it, and live among them," and McLaren describes having found them. Sources and verification: 2026-09-10, from the fetched page text held in SKS. Both are at one remove and the sheet does not hide it — the Gray-Hammond copy is a bookmark capture rather than the live page, and the McLaren passage reaches us through the Stimpunks Empathy glossary, which is our own compilation. Each is a first-hand account by its author, quoted with the author named and linked, and neither is load-bearing for a fact — they are testimony that the experience is reported, which is what the sheet claims of them. Our own prior art on hyperempathy, and a splice not to inherit Quoted on: Other People Who Have It, Sheet No. 10, which cites the Stimpunks Foundation's Justice Sensitivity, Autistic Joy, Glimmers and Empathy glossary pages as ours. This sheet continues an argument Stimpunks has already made, and says so. The Canary and Very Grand Emotions glossary pages have paired Butler's biological conscience with Autistic "cultural immune system" claims for years. Presenting the pairing as new would have been the site's own failure mode aimed at itself. AND THOSE TWO PAGES CARRY A SPLICE THIS SHEET MUST NOT INHERIT. Both present "I wish I could find other people who have it, and live among them. A biological conscience is better than no conscience at all" and "Maybe it's like my sharing: One more weirdness…" as a single blockquote under a single citation. The two are about ninety pages apart and in the wrong order — Kindle locations 1565 and 350. The splice changes the meaning. In context Lauren is comparing her emerging Earthseed conviction to her hyperempathy: the "one more weirdness… that I'm stuck with" is the religion, and hyperempathy is what she measures it against. Joined to the biological-conscience line it reads as though the weirdness she is stuck with is the conscience itself. Every word is Butler's, every sentence is exact, and the quotation says something Butler did not. Not fixable from this repository. Recorded in DECISIONS.md for a session in the SKS repository, with the paths. This sheet quotes the two passages separately or not at all. Why this quotation is load-bearing rather than illustrative. It is the one source on the sheet that is neither a poem nor a scholar, and it is the only one describing what the metaphor costs. The sheet's hinge — that an armour which costs nothing to deploy is also the reason nobody believes you need support — is Liv's observation and not King's, and King's poem only turns out to contain it once you have read Liv. The fox-and-hedgehog pairing with monotropism has no first use we can find Relied on, and flagged as unattributed, on: Two Cohabitating Modes. The sheet reports that the hedgehog's one big thing and the fox's many things have been mapped onto monotropism and polytropism in neurodivergent writing and talking. We have not found who did that first, and the sheet says so in those words. Two things are established and the join between them is not. Berlin does not mention attention, autism, or anything of the kind — he is sorting novelists and philosophers. Murray, Lesser and Lawson (2005) does not mention foxes or hedgehogs. The pairing is a later, informal synthesis circulating in community spaces, podcasts and conversation. Monotropism was coined by Dinah Murray with her neighbour Jeanette Buirski, and set out in Murray, Lesser and Lawson (2005), Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism, Autism 9(2), 139–156, <https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361305051398>. The paper has not been read here and nothing is quoted from it — the citation is pinned from Crossref, as it is for the entry on monotropa-uniflora.html. The third author is Wenn Lawson and the journal's byline reads "Wendy Lawson"; see that entry for why we cite him as Wenn and state what the byline says. The one instance the sheet cites is cited as an instance. The Fox and the Hedgehog: On Neurodiversity, episode Rethinking Scientific Minds, 2 June 2025, as listed by podcast.app and credited there to Linda MacDonald Glenn. The episode has not been listened to, the description reads as promotional copy, and the caption on the sheet says outright that it is evidence the pairing circulates and not a source for the claim. Nothing on the page rests on it. Open: a first use in print or in a talk. If one exists, the sheet should credit it. Archilochus, at two removes, and no Greek edition opened Referred to on: Two Cohabitating Modes. The sheet gives the proverb as "the fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing" and credits Archilochus, a seventh-century poet and soldier from Paros. NO GREEK EDITION HAS BEEN OPENED HERE, AND THE SHEET SAYS SO. The English above is a rendering in circulation, reaching the page through Isaiah Berlin's essay on Tolstoy by way of the Vanhuysse review above — which we did read. It is therefore at two removes, and it is presented as a rendering rather than as a translation this site can vouch for. The Greek is deliberately not set: it would be an unverified transcription, and the two house faces have no greek subset, so it would render in a system fallback like the Sappho on /flower-codes. What would upgrade it: a Greek text of the fragment with an editor and a numbering, and a named translator for whichever English is used. Open, at one remove and carried inside somebody else's quotation: Vanhuysse says the distinction "was further elaborated during the Renaissance by Erasmus of Rotterdam". The Adagia have not been consulted. The claim is on his authority, inside his quotation, and the sheet flags it as unresolved. Two lines quoted from living authors, and one word of Sagan's changed in our own masthead Quoted on: Two Cohabitating Modes, one sentence each, in copyright, quoted with attribution. Carl Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark (1995), of his parents: "But in introducing me simultaneously to skepticism and to wonder, they taught me the two uneasily cohabiting modes of thought that are central to the scientific method." Dorion Sagan, Cosmic Apprentice: Dispatches from the Edges of Science (University of Minnesota Press, 2013): "Science's eye for detail, buttressed by philosophy's broad view, makes for a kind of alembic, an antidote to both." Both are quoted from Ryan's own reading and both are also on Star Stuff's Who Is Holding the Candle. Neither page has been re-opened for this sheet and both captions say so. THE PAGE'S TITLE IS OURS AND NOT SAGAN'S, BY ONE SYLLABLE. Sagan wrote cohabiting. The sheet is called Two Cohabitating Modes — Ryan's title, and the word is a real one. The difference does not change the meaning, and it is still a difference, so by this site's own rule the title is an adaptation and not a quotation: if we changed the words, they are ours. The sheet states this in a note beside the specimen, and the specimen itself carries Sagan's sentence unaltered. Logged here because the rule has to survive contact with our own masthead, which is the one place nobody thinks to check — the same failure found in our own foundation's rendering of the Playful Manifesto, one preposition wide. Stimpunks' own page on scientism, and a stacked list that is a summary of it Quoted on: Two Cohabitating Modes, one paragraph, whole. Stimpunks Foundation, Facts, Fire, and Feels: Research-Storytelling from the Edges. Read at source 2026-09-10. Ours, and still cited, because a house source quoted without a citation is the pattern that produced the Playful Manifesto drift. The bold is the page's own and is reproduced. Ryan's brief carried the same idea as a stacked list — "Science + Philosophy / Skepticism + Wonder / Empiricism + Voice / Bio + Psycho + Social / Body + Mind / Bodyminds" — which also appears on that page. The prose is what the sheet quotes, because the stacked form is a summary device and the sentences are the claim. Quoting the list instead would have been a tightening in the other direction: the same words, with the argument taken out from between them. Thomas Bewick, two wood engravings and two sentences, 1792 Mounted on: Two Cohabitating Modes — .qe-plate-wide in the hedgehog section and in the fox section, each with a .qe-specimen quoting the article it heads. Thomas Bewick (1753–1828), wood engravings, in A General History of Quadrupeds (Newcastle upon Tyne: printed by and for S. Hodgson, R. Beilby & T. Bewick, 1792) — the hedgehog on page 448 and the Cur Fox on page 280. Public domain: the work is 1792, and a faithful photographic reproduction of a two-dimensional public-domain work attracts no new copyright. Scanned by Smithsonian Libraries for the Biodiversity Heritage Library, Internet Archive item generalhistory00bewi, 504 images. The Archive record carries no rights statement and no licence URL; the age of the work is what settles it. Read, cropped and re-encoded here on 2026-09-10 — tools/make-plates.py, the wide ladder, the filename carrying the provenance. The quotations, verified off the page images rather than the scan's text layer: Two transcription decisions, both stated in the captions. The long s of the 1792 setting is transcribed as s — the page reads "fpinous", "fecures", "beafts", "leaft", "moft" — which is a letterform and not a different letter. And "harrassed" is the printing's own spelling and is kept, on the same footing as King's "runts". THE HEADING IS THE SUBJECT OF THE SENTENCE, AND THAT IS WHY BOTH QUOTATIONS BEGIN MID-GRAMMAR. Bewick sets the engraving, then the article's name, then a drop capital running straight on: The Hedge-hog, or Urchin, / "is provided by Nature with a spinous armour". Quoting from the drop capital gives a sentence with no subject, so the captions say where the subject is rather than silently supplying one in brackets. The Greyhound Fox cut on page 279 was looked at and passed over, because it shows a fox with a kill — and a predation scene is the one thing the drawings on this page must not say, for the reason the tray mark's two animals face the same way. One thing the caption has to say because the book is wrong about it. Bewick gives "three varieties of Foxes in this island" — Greyhound, Mastiff and Cur — and they are not three species. All are Vulpes vulpes; the division is an eighteenth-century sorting by size and build. Mounting "The Cur Fox" without saying so would let a reader take a retired taxonomy for a live one, on the authority of our page rather than his.

records.heading: Open
records.text: Who wrote the crooked tree — Waits, the screenplay, or Keret Drawn after on: index.html, #to-queer-is-to-adapt. Phrase quoted: four words, <q>growing strong and growing strange</q>. The monologue is spoken by Tom Waits, as Kneller, in Wristcutters: A Love Story (2006), written and directed by Goran Dukić, adapted from Etgar Keret's novella Kneller's Happy Campers. A straight tree spends its life telling a crooked one what it is; the lumberjacks arrive and are told to cut all the straight trees; the crooked one is still there. What is not established is who wrote it. It is widely repeated online that Waits improvised the speech, and we have not found that claim in a primary source — not in an interview with Waits, not with Dukić, and not in the published screenplay. It is equally possible it is Dukić's writing, or that it descends from Keret. A drawing does not require the answer, which is why the figure is captioned as spoken by Waits and makes no claim about authorship. But the site quotes four of the words, and four words have an author. What would settle it: the screenplay, or an interview where Waits or Dukić says whose it is. Until then the caption says what we know — who said it, in what, directed by whom, from whose story — and says openly that we do not know who wrote it. Why this is Open and not Verified. The tempting move was to caption it "Tom Waits" and let a reader assume he wrote what he said. That is this site's characteristic failure in miniature: an attribution that is true about the speaking and silent about the writing, left to be read as a claim about both. Two sentences on the Miranda sheet claim a little more than their source does On: the-tempest.html, second paragraph. Found: 2026-09-08, while verifying the draft. Left as sent — fixing either means changing Helen's words, which is not this session's call. Neither is an invented source. Both are the failure CLAUDE.md names as this site's characteristic one: a source tightened rather than fabricated, with the attribution left attached. 1. "the first recorded use of it as a person's name in English (Wikipedia contributors, n.d.)" The cited article) says Shakespeare "originated use of the name as a forename", and says in the same breath that Miranda existed as a surname before him. A surname is a person's name. So the sheet's sentence is a step wider than the source it credits, and the source contains the counter-example. The narrower claim — that Shakespeare coined it as a given name — is what Wikipedia supports and is the interesting claim anyway. Suggested fix, for Helen and Ryan: "the first recorded use of it as a given name in English." One word, and the citation becomes true. 2. "He built it from the Latin gerundive of mirari, to wonder at" The gerundive derivation is correct Latin — mirandus, -a, -um is the gerundive of mirari, and "she who is to be wondered at" is a fair rendering of it. It is simply not in the cited source: Wikipedia says only "from the Latin word mirandus" and never mentions the gerundive or mirari. So the Latin is ours, and it is standing inside a sentence that reads as Wikipedia's. It wants either a Latin dictionary behind it or a sentence break that puts the citation on the half it actually covers. Why this is worth an entry rather than a quiet edit. The sheet's title turns on this etymology — To Be Wondered With is a one-preposition move on to be wondered at — so the gerundive is not a decorative aside, it is the load-bearing claim of the whole sheet, and it is the one claim on the page with nothing verified under it. The wrong violet is mounted on the flower codes sheet On: flower-codes.html, first plate. Found: 2026-09-08, while choosing the plates. Mounted anyway, with the problem in the caption. The violet the sheet is about is the Mediterranean sweet violet, Viola odorata. The plate mounted is Viola pedata, the American birdfoot violet, photographed for a New York state museum survey in 1918. It was the public-domain violet plate to hand. The caption carries the correction — "This is not Sappho's violet… The plant is the genus, not the poem" — so nothing on the page claims otherwise, and a note at the foot of the sheet asks readers for a better plate. The fix is one line of markup and a new caption the day a public-domain Viola odorata plate turns up. Until then this is the only object on the site standing in for a different object, and it is doing so out loud.

The mission lists what this cabinet is for and names the page keeping each aim. This is the argument underneath them. It is adapted from a manifesto about learning spaces — written by the two people who make this site together with seven others, and licensed for exactly this — carried off that subject and pointed at reading instead.

records.heading: This begins and does not end
records.text: Specimen — how a manifesto opens Quoted whole, and here is why that is worth a note The version of these sentences that circulates — including on our own foundation’s page — runs them together as a translation of my world into yours….This is a protest. Alexander wrote to yours, and three sentences stand between that one and the protest. One preposition and an ellipsis — which is precisely the size of the failure this site keeps a ledger to catch, and it is instructive that we found it in our own house first. Logged there. Two of those sentences are the whole of our position, and we are taking the move rather than the words. A protest of the notion that there is any correct way to live is what a queering lens is for. A rejection of the idea that one’s usefulness is a measure of their humanity is why the readings here keep arriving at illness, at refusal, at lying down. And a manifesto that begins but will never end is the right shape for a cabinet. There is no last sheet, because there is no last thing that could have been otherwise.

records.heading: Normal is an arrangement, and arrangements have authors
records.text: The word is barely two centuries old in the sense everyone now uses it. It arrived with the statistician rather than the physician, and it displaced older words that meant something else entirely: wyrd meant fate — what befalls you — before it was demoted to weird and then to defect. A thing that was invented can be read as an invention. That is a different act from complaining about it, and a much more useful one. Somebody arranged this. The arrangement has a date, a discipline and a set of interests behind it, and every one of those is legible if you go and look. So we do not accept that the way things are arranged is the way things are. Not in a canon, not in a diagnosis, not in a syllabus, and not in the sentence you were handed about what your body is for. Sheet No. 4 is that history at length; this is the claim it licences.

records.heading: Weird is a verb
records.text: The site’s own word is queering, taken from Nick Walker as a verb and not a noun. He has said the same of weird, and the pairing is the reason Sheet No. 4 exists. Specimen — weirding, as a verb A crack in the normal is what a reading is. Not a demolition — nobody here is arguing that The Tempest should not have been written, or that Woolf was wrong about her own illness. A crack is narrower and more useful than that: it is the place where the arrangement admits it is one.

quotes.text: And so weird, I think about it like the word Queer, as a verb. There’s this act of weirding, of letting the Magic in, of making cracks in the normal to let all the magic in.
quotes.source: Nick Walker, in conversation on the Weird Pride Day panel of David’s Divergent Discussions. Quoted from the transcription in the Neuroqueer Learning Spaces Manifesto, which describes it as edited, and not checked here against the recording. The citation is the transcription, not the tape.

records.heading: Whose reading is allowed to count
records.text: A canon is not only a list of works. It is a settled set of readings of those works, and the settling was done by particular people under particular conditions. Grada Kilomba puts the mechanism in two lines that need no gloss. Specimen — the hierarchy in the words Interpretation is where that hierarchy is enforced, so interpretation is where it can be contested. This site’s method — a reading, cited to the primary, signed by whoever made it, with the working left in — is not neutral procedure. It is a claim that a reading made from a bodymind the canon was not written for is a reading, and not merely an experience.

quotes.text:
They have facts, we have opinions.
They have knowledges, we have experiences.
quotes.source: Grada Kilomba, Who Can Speak?, in Decolonizing Knowledge (2016). Quoted from the rendering in the Neuroqueer Learning Spaces Manifesto; the primary has not been read here. Two contiguous lines of a longer passage, so nothing is elided inside the quotation.

records.heading: The method is the argument
records.text: Everything this cabinet does procedurally is also something it is asserting. We cite to the primary because they have facts, we have opinions is answered by producing the fact. We publish every correction because a reading that cannot be wrong is not a reading, it is a ruling — the thing we object to, wearing our own coat. We sign the reading and name the maker separately because collapsing them is how an interpretation becomes the work. We make it printable, and legible in two grounds, and free because an argument about who is allowed to read is not made by a page somebody cannot read. None of that is generosity. It is the argument, carried out in the only form that can carry it.

records.heading: What we refuse
records.text: That a text has one reading and somebody already found it. A work that can be read only one way has stopped being a work and become a ruling. That a source can be tightened to fit. Trim a definition to fit a masthead and leave the name attached, and you have written somebody else’s sentence for them. If we changed the words, they are ours. That usefulness measures a person. Alexander’s sentence, and the reason illness and refusal keep turning up on the plate. That access is a favour. Plain view is not a concession to somebody else; it is one of the two ways this site is meant to be read. That a finished thing should hide how it was made. The register, the ledger and the decision log are all public, including the parts where we were wrong. That this could be completed. See above, and see Alexander.

records.heading: Where this comes from
records.text: Most of the frame above is adapted from the Neuroqueer Learning Spaces Manifesto, a community project initiated by Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar — the two people who make this site — together with seven other contributors: David Gray-Hammond, Kay Louise Aldred, Dan Aldred, Pernille Fraser, Max Alexander, Je’anna Clements and Jorn Bettin. It is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, which is why this adaptation exists and why this page carries the same licence. Why the credit is not a formality Two of that manifesto’s authors also wrote this page, and it would be easy to treat the whole thing as ours to carry across. It is not. Nine people wrote it, its argument about learning spaces is theirs collectively, and what has been done here is to take that argument off its subject and point it at reading — which is an adaptation, and adaptations get named. The share-alike clause is not a technicality either: it is the reason this site can do this at all, and the reason anyone may do the same to this page. The original is about classrooms, bodyminds and who holds a space. This is about texts, canons and who settled a reading. The shared claim is the one worth carrying: that the arrangement is an arrangement, that the people it was not built for are the ones who can see its edges, and that nothing about it was inevitable.

This site has a page for what it holds, a page for how it is made, a page for everything it has got wrong, and a page for what it knows about you. What it did not have was a page saying, plainly and in one place, what we are trying to do. That absence is not neutral: a project with no stated aim is a project whose aims can drift without anybody being able to point at the drift — which is the same objection this site makes to a quotation nobody can trace, or a number nobody can re-derive.

records.heading: The whole of it, in one sentence
records.text: Queering Earth reads the canon closely and in public — art, literature, poetry, politics, people, and history — and asks what else any of it could have been, so that the arrangements we were handed stop looking like the only ones available. Thirteen aims follow, in four groups. None of them is a hope. Each one names a page where it is already being practised, because a values list you cannot check against the work is the exact thing this page is trying not to be. And the last section names, for each, the observation that would show we had quietly stopped.

records.heading: What we are claiming
records.text:
Queering is a verb. The word reaches us from Queer Theory by way of Nick Walker, and what we took is the parenthesis: subverting, defying, disrupting, liberating oneself from. It names something you do to a norm, not a category you belong to, and the norms it can be done to are not only the ones about sex and gender. A site that used the word as a synonym for a demographic would be using the noun and calling it the verb.
 Kept on Queering is a verb, where he is quoted exactly rather than paraphrased. Normal is an invention, and a recent one. Barely two centuries old, arriving with the statistician rather than the physician, and it displaced older words that meant something else entirely — wyrd meant fate, what befalls you, before it was demoted to weird and then to defect. A thing that was invented can be read as an invention, which is a different act from complaining about it.
 Kept on Sheet No. 4, and it is Helen Edgar’s reading before it is this site’s. Having been canonised is not the same as having been settled. Every sheet takes a work that has already been decided about and asks what else it could have been. Not to catch anybody out — the readings here are affectionate, and several are love letters. But a text that can only be read one way has stopped being a text and become a ruling.
 Kept on the plate, one sheet at a time.

records.heading: How we intend to be right
records.text:
Interpretation is the method, and the room left open is the product. There are no hard facts here for everything, and that is the design brief rather than a lowered bar. Our sibling Star Stuff is built on evidence and risks a wrong fact; this half of the shelf is built on reading and risks a wrong attribution. What replaces the fact is not licence. It is the obligation to show the reading’s working, so that somebody can disagree with it precisely rather than vaguely.
 Kept on What this is, and argued in full on the colophon. If we changed the words, they are ours. The characteristic failure on a site like this is not an invented source. It is a tightened one — a definition trimmed to fit a masthead, an object quietly generalised, a paraphrase left wearing somebody’s name. So: credit the concept, quote the original exactly, or write our own line. When we carry somebody’s idea to an object they were not writing about, the sheet says whose move that is instead of letting their authority cover our argument.
 Kept in the attribution ledger — see the Tuck and Yang entry, where the transposition is named on the sheet in a sentence of its own. Every quotation reaches the page from a primary, or names whose transcription it is. A search of our own library is not verification: five files agreeing with each other are one witness, not five. Where the primary can be reached we read it and say which copy, because that is how an edition difference gets caught. Where it cannot, the quotation carries the citation and the name of whoever transcribed it, rather than being dropped or quietly smoothed.
 Kept in the ledger, each entry dated the day a person read the source. Publish the corrections, and spend the gold on the mend. Every sheet carries at its foot the date it was mounted and the number of times we have corrected it since, each clause linked to the entry that did it. The seam is marked in the most expensive colour the palette has, because kintsugi is not that the crack shows — it is that the precious material goes on the break. A register with no corrections in it is not a clean record. It is a record nobody is keeping. Kept in the accession register, and on the provenance line at the foot of every sheet. A reading is signed, and the reader is not the maker. Woolf made On Being Ill; we made the reading of it. Those are two different people, on two different rows of the label and in two different fields of the machine-readable copy, and no page here collapses them into one name at the top. Getting that wrong would tell every agent on the web that we wrote Woolf.
 Kept on Who reads, and who writes, and enforced by a gate that refuses the conflation.

records.heading: What we owe whoever is reading
records.text:
One document, and two ways to read it. The type here leans, deviates, and refuses to sit on the line, because a page about normativity set in a tidy grid is arguing against itself. All of that lives in the stylesheet, over ordinary semantic markup, and plain view switches it off. Never an image of text. Never a decorative copy beside an accessible one — two copies of the same words drift, and the accessible one is always the copy that rots.
 Kept on Plain view, and on the control at the top of this page. Accessibility measured, not asserted. Contrast is held at 7:1 in both grounds and under print emulation — the house target, not the 4.5:1 floor. Every page has one landmark, real headings, an address for every section, and a printable sheet. None of that is a promise: each claim is checked by a gate that runs before anything ships, and the gates are in the repository where you can run them yourself.
 Kept on How it is built, and in the tools directory. Ask nothing of you. No analytics, no cookies, no accounts, no comments, no advertising, no newsletter gate, and nothing fetched from anybody else’s server unless you press something that says so first. The one field on the site never submits anywhere, and what you search for stays in your own browser.
 Kept on What this site knows about you, which is checked against the code every time the code grows a capability.

records.heading: How we work
records.text:
In public, with the working-out left in. The pages, the drawings, the tools, the gates, the attribution ledger, the decision log and every error we have caught in our own work are one public repository at one commit. The register records not only what we mounted but what we took down again and why. Nothing here is finished in private and then presented.
 Kept in the repository and in the register. Free, forkable, and yes to the machines. Everything of ours is CC BY-SA 4.0; the works we read belong to the people who made them and were never ours to license. The training crawlers and the retrieval crawlers are named in robots.txt and allowed, because a refusal beside a share-alike licence would be a contradiction somebody would eventually have to resolve. The answer is yes and the ask is attribution — so the citation trail is published in the form a machine can actually reach.
 Kept in robots.txt, in llms.txt, and in a Markdown copy beside every page.

records.heading: What a cabinet of readings has to do with Stimpunks
records.text: Queering Earth is a collaboration between the Stimpunks Foundation and More Realms. Stimpunks is a 501(c)(3) with a mission of its own, published on its own site, and it is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing — the paraphrase is where a mission usually goes soft, and paraphrase-wearing-a-name is the failure this whole site is organised against. Specimen — the foundation’s own words The middle sentence has three verbs in it, and this site is a contribution to each one. Live with dignity is what a reading does when it hands somebody a word for themselves that is not a deficit. Challenge dehumanizing systems is what Sheet No. 4 does to normal and Sheet No. 1 does to the army you desert by lying down. Design environments that honor difference as strength is the reason the type on this site plays and the reason plain view exists in the same breath. The third sentence is the one that surprised us. Stimpunks’ own mission says weird — and Sheet No. 4 is the history of exactly that word being demoted from wyrd, meaning fate, to a name for people who do not fit. The sheet was not written to illustrate the mission. It turned out to be about it.

quotes.text:
We exist for the direct support and mutual aid of neurodivergent and disabled people.

Stimpunks builds accessible infrastructure and public tools that support disabled and neurodivergent people to live with dignity, challenge dehumanizing systems, and design environments that honor difference as strength.

We enable the weird, feral, chaotic, and magical people.
quotes.source: Stimpunks Foundation, Mission, read 9 September 2026. Their capitalisation and their spelling.

records.heading: And what it has to do with More Realms
records.text: The other half is Helen Edgar’s, and her own landing page states the method this site borrowed before this site existed. Specimen — the other masthead Not a place of conclusions or answers is the same commitment this site makes when it says there are no hard facts here for everything, arrived at from her side rather than ours. The tagline on the masthead is hers — post-normal possibilities, written in the founding brainstorm — and the masthead credits Nick Walker beneath it because his book carries the phrase as a subtitle, one hyphen apart. That credit is not an admission of borrowing and does not claim one; it is what you do when a collision is real and a reader will eventually find it.

quotes.text: This is not a place of conclusions or answers, it’s a place to wander, to feel, to think sideways, expand, explore and be inspired.
quotes.source: Helen Edgar, More Realms, landing page, read 9 September 2026. Her punctuation.

records.heading: The limit, said plainly
records.text: What this site does not do Stimpunks’ first programme is direct financial support to individuals — rent, medical bills, equipment, creator grants, living wages. This site does none of that and should not be counted as though it did. No sheet here has paid anybody’s rent or replaced anybody’s wheelchair. If anything on these pages is worth something to you, the thing that converts it into material help is the foundation, not the artifact. The honest claim for a cabinet of readings is narrower, and still worth making. It is what somebody can reach at two in the morning, free, without an account, in a browser, when they have just been told again that the way they are is a defect — and find a page that takes the question seriously enough to cite its sources.

records.heading: How you could tell if we stopped
records.text: An aim you cannot fail is not an aim. Each of these is a condition somebody could observe from outside, with no access to what we meant, which is the only sort of accountability worth publishing. The aim, and the observation that would falsify it Aim What would show we had stopped Queering is a verb The word used here as a synonym for a demographic, or as something a person is rather than something done to a norm. Canonised is not settled A sheet that arrives at the verdict the work already had, and adds nothing to it but agreement. The room left open A sheet that closes its reading — that tells you what the poem means rather than what it could mean, and leaves you nothing to disagree with. If we changed the words A quotation here that does not match its source, with the source’s name still attached. Or our extension of somebody’s idea presented as their reach rather than ours. Primary sources A citation trail that ends at a quote site, an encyclopedia, one of our own pages, or a machine’s summary. Publish the corrections A stretch of the register with no corrections in it. We are not that good; a clean run means we stopped looking. Reader is not the maker A page whose byline or metadata names us as the author of the work being read. One document Anything readable only in the decorated version, or an image with words in it that the words are not also in. Measured, not asserted A contrast failure shipped and left standing, a page that comes off a printer blank, or a gate quietly run without its checking flag. Ask nothing of you Any request to a third party that the reader did not choose, or any attempt to find out who is reading. In public A count printed in our prose that nobody can re-derive from the repository. Most of those are not hypothetical, and the ones that have already happened here are the reason the list reads the way it does. This site’s working tagline was once a paraphrase of Nick Walker wearing his name, and it was replaced. Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang were carried from settler colonialism to masking, and the sheet nearly let their authority cover the move before it was made to say so in a sentence of its own. The plate said Seven sheets above eight cards for as long as the eighth had been up — a count in our prose that nobody could re-derive, which is the last row of that table, committed by us, on this site, and found only because somebody read down the page and counted. Every one of those is in the register with a date on it. That is the point of keeping one.

records.heading: Who wrote this, and with what
records.text: The reading, the editing, and the deciding are Helen Edgar’s and Ryan Boren’s; the drafting is done in sessions with an AI assistant, directed and edited by whichever of them is answerable for the sheet. A tool does not get a row on the label, because a byline is responsibility and a tool cannot carry any — but a site that keeps a ledger of everybody else’s words owes an honest account of where its own came from, so the arrangement is described rather than left to be inferred. The full statement, including what is never allowed to stand as a citation, is on the colophon.

Specimen Monotropa uniflora L. — the ghost pipe, the Indian pipe, the ghost plant Named Carl Linnaeus, Species Plantarum, 1753. Monotropa, one turn, for the arched stem; uniflora, one-flowered Also mounted Emily Dickinson to Mabel Loomis Todd, 30 September 1882 (Letter 997), and Dickinson’s poem ‘Tis whiter than an Indian pipe, about 1879 (Fr1513A) Following Helen Edgar, Monotropa Uniflora and Monotropism, More Realms, 7 July 2026 — written for the fifth anniversary of Dinah Murray’s death, and the reason this sheet exists Read 9 September 2026 Read by Ryan Boren Biology Not here. The mechanism — myco-heterotrophy, carbon taken from fungi and none given back — is our sibling site’s: Star Stuff, A Field Guide to Symbioses. This sheet has the naming, the letter, the poem, and the word Terms Monotropism · Neuroqueer · Interdependence · Flow state There is a plant in the deep shade of North American, Latin American and East Asian forests that carries no green at all. It cannot photosynthesise. It does not reach for the light. It draws everything it needs from fungal threads in the soil, which draw theirs from the roots of trees — so the plant lives, entirely, on a connection nobody above ground can see. Linnaeus named it in 1753 for the single turn of its stem. Emily Dickinson pressed it into a herbarium, wrote a poem about it, and called it the preferred flower of life. Two hundred and thirty-eight years after the naming, an Autistic researcher and her neighbour reached for the same Greek root to describe a mind whose attention runs in one deep channel instead of many shallow ones.

records.heading: Seven hands on one specimen
records.text: This sheet is a wall rather than a reading, and the difference is not decoration. A reading has an order and an argument that arrives at the end. A wall has a chorus: many people, across two hundred and seventy years, standing in front of the same object and each seeing something the others could not. A herbarium sheet that has been in a cabinet long enough looks exactly like this — a specimen, and a stack of determination slips in different hands, every one of them signed.

quotes.text: That without suspecting it you should send me the preferred flower of life, seems almost supernatural, and the sweet glee that I felt at meeting it, I could confide to none.
quotes.source: Emily Dickinson to Mabel Loomis Todd, 30 September 1882 — Letter 997, in pencil. Todd had sent her a painted panel of Indian pipes six days earlier.

quotes.text:
This limitless Hyperbole
Each one of us shall be -
‘Tis Drama - if Hypothesis
It be not Tragedy -
quotes.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘Tis whiter than an Indian pipe, about 1879 — the last quatrain, from R. W. Franklin’s reading of Amherst Manuscript 483 (Fr1513A).

quotes.text: He meant, perhaps, that the androgynous mind is resonant and porous; that it transmits emotion without impediment; that it is naturally creative, incandescent and undivided.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, chapter VI (Hogarth Press, 1929), pp. 148–149. The he is Coleridge, and Woolf is guessing at what he meant — twice, with a perhaps in each clause.

quotes.text: Attention without feeling, I began to learn, is only a report. An openness — an empathy — was necessary if the attention was to matter.
quotes.source: Mary Oliver, Our World (Beacon Press, 2007). Transcribed by Ryan Boren from his own copy. Not from Upstream, which is where this sentence is usually credited — see the label correction below.

quotes.text: I haven’t really ever had a career, I’ve had a mission.
quotes.source: Dinah Murray, interviewed by Kate Fox in Dalgety Bay about a month before her death on 7 July 2021, quoted in Fox’s tribute, 16 August 2021. Fox titled the poem she read at the memorial Monotropa Uniflora.

quotes.text: It is a plant that refuses to be binary at the root of its being, in the same way it refuses to draw its nourishment from sunlight, the way other plants are expected to.
quotes.source: Helen Edgar, Monotropa Uniflora and Monotropism, More Realms, July 2026. Monotropa uniflora is a perfect flower in the botanical sense — stamens and pistil in one bloom.

quotes.text: The quality of presence that the world persistently mistakes for absence, the inner life that runs deeper than it appears from the outside?
quotes.source: Helen Edgar, same essay, on what the it of Dickinson’s poem might be. Her sentence ends in a question mark and it is left here, because she is asking rather than concluding.

records.heading: One root, three turns
records.text: The Greek monotropos means turning one way. Linnaeus took it for the arched stem of a flower. Two centuries later two women in London took it for a mind. Nobody planned the rhyme, and it is not a metaphor either: it is the same word, describing the same shape twice. monotropos Greek Turning one way; of a single turn. Monos, one, and tropos, a turn — the same tropos that gives English trope, a turn of phrase. Monotropa 1753 Linnaeus’s genus, in Species Plantarum. The turn is physical: the stem arches over so the single flower hangs facing the ground. A plant named for the direction it bends. monotropism 1991 onward Attention pooled in one deep channel rather than spread thin across many. Coined by Dinah Murray with her neighbour Jeanette Buirski, and set out in Murray, Lesser and Lawson’s 2005 paper. A turn you are, not a turn you make. The 2005 paper is Murray, Lesser and Lawson, Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism, in Autism 9(2), 139–156. Its third author is Wenn Lawson, and the journal’s byline still reads Wendy Lawson. He is a trans man who has published under Wenn for years, and a citation that reproduces a publisher’s record over a living author’s own name is not neutral accuracy — it is a database outranking a person. We cite him as Wenn Lawson and say what the byline says, so a reader can find the paper and nobody has to be deadnamed to do it.

records.heading: Two hands, and one of them is the same hand
records.text: Mabel Loomis Todd painted a panel of Indian pipes and sent it to Emily Dickinson in September 1882. Dickinson wrote back within days, in pencil, and told her she had sent the preferred flower of life. Eight years later, when Todd and T. W. Higginson brought out the first posthumous Poems, that painting went on the cover. Todd is also one of the two editors who tidied Dickinson. Sheet No. 6 is about what they did to Wild nights: Higginson wrote let us alter as little as possible and then printed the poem with eight of its nine dashes gone. The hand that gave Dickinson her favourite flower is the hand that regularised her punctuation. That is not hypocrisy and it is not a scandal — it is what editing was, and Todd is the reason a great deal of Dickinson survived at all. It is simply worth saying that the same person can be the gift and the alteration, and that a reader who only has the tidied text cannot tell. Gift and alteration, one hand.

records.heading: A poem, and what 1896 did to it
records.text: Three years before the letter, Dickinson had already written the plant down. The poem survives on a fragment of stationery, in pencil, about 1879. She left herself alternatives, and the first editors took them. Franklin records three words Dickinson wrote in as options: denote for imply in line 5, designate for intimate in line 6, and What customs for What function in line 8. When the poem was first printed in Poems (1896) it appeared as three quatrains, with the alternatives for lines 5 and 8 adopted — so the version that circulated read denote and What customs, and the version above is the one on the paper. Neither reading is a mistake. She wrote both. But an editor choosing between a poet’s alternatives, silently, and printing the result as the poem is the same move as removing her dashes, and it is the move this collection keeps finding. The alternatives are the poem too. A text that has had its options resolved for you is a text with a decision hidden in it. ‘Tis Drama — if Hypothesis It be not Tragedy

quotes.text:
‘Tis whiter than an Indian Pipe -
‘Tis dimmer than a Lace -
No stature has it, like a Fog
When you approach the place -
Not any voice imply it here -
Or intimate it there -
A spirit - how doth it accost -
What function hath the Air?
This limitless Hyperbole
Each one of us shall be -
‘Tis Drama - if Hypothesis
It be not Tragedy -
quotes.source: Emily Dickinson, about 1879. Amherst Manuscript 483, in pencil on a fragment of stationery. Text from R. W. Franklin, The Poems of Emily Dickinson: Variorum Edition (Belknap Press, 1998), Fr1513A, as published in the Emily Dickinson Archive.

records.heading: She kept a herbarium, which is what this site is
records.text: Dickinson assembled more than four hundred pressed plants as a young woman, mounted and labelled, and the album is now in Harvard’s Houghton Library — the same library that holds the manuscript on Sheet No. 6. Monotropa uniflora is in it. This site is drawn as a herbarium sheet because the form makes an attribution argument: a specimen is somebody else’s, a label is where we speak, and the line between them is drawn in the layout rather than left to a reader’s good faith. It is a slightly strange thing to discover that the poet on two of our sheets was doing the same thing at nineteen, with real plants, in an album, in Amherst. Which is also the answer to the question people keep asking about her life. From outside it looked like a withdrawal. From the letters, the poems, and four hundred labelled specimens, it looks like the opposite: attention pooled, at length, on a small number of things, with enormous care. There is a word for that now, and the word shares a root with the flower.

records.heading: Not a tragedy
records.text:
The plant is white because it has given up chlorophyll. It has no leaves. It grows in the dark, on the forest floor, out of leaf litter, and it feeds through fungi that feed through trees. By every measure a plant is usually judged by, it is failing at being a plant. It is also perfectly well. It is not a parasite on trees and not a saprophyte on rot, which is what botanists thought for a century; it is a myco-heterotroph, and the arrangement works. The plant is not doing without a connection to light. It is connected to light through somebody else. That is not a lesser way to be alive, and Star Stuff has the numbers on how the carbon actually moves. Dickinson’s last line does not say the thing is a tragedy. It says: ‘Tis Drama - if Hypothesis / It be not Tragedy - — which reads, turned around, as a hope with a condition on it. Helen puts the same thought without the subjunctive: the ghost pipe is not a tragedy, and neither are Autistic people, and both thrive when the conditions are right rather than when they are corrected. What this sheet will not tidy We are not claiming Dickinson was Autistic, and neither is Helen — she says so in as many words on her own page. Monotropism is a theory of attention that many Autistic people recognise; a nineteenth-century poet cannot be assessed by resemblance, and reading her life through a word coined in 1991 is our doing, not hers. The rhyme between the plant and the theory is a coincidence of vocabulary, not evidence of anything. Linnaeus named a stem’s curve. Murray and Buirski named a pattern of attention. That both reached for monotropos is lovely and it proves nothing about either. This sheet has no plate. Every mounted image on this site is public domain — botanical prints, a painting, a manuscript leaf, and two wood engravings — and we do not have one of Monotropa uniflora. The Dickinson manuscript is available but licensed, the modern photographs are in copyright, and Todd’s painted panel — the object at the centre of the letter — we could not clear. If you know of a public-domain Monotropa uniflora plate, it belongs here. Say so and it will be. The plant blackens and collapses when handled, and Helen reads that as recognisable. We have kept her reading in her words rather than generalising it, because maybe it’s just me who relates in this way is in her sentence and taking it out would make a shared claim out of a personal one. The biology here is deliberately thin. Myco-heterotrophy is a mechanism with numbers attached and those belong to our sibling site, which risks a wrong fact where this one risks a wrong attribution. If you want to know how the carbon moves, go there. Dinah Murray spent her last years photographing lichens and mushrooms on the Fife coast — the same kingdom of organisms this plant lives through, attended to closely, for their own sake, by someone who had given the world a word for exactly that kind of attention. Kate Fox called the memorial poem Monotropa Uniflora. It was the right name. Provenance
 Mounted 9 September 2026.
 Label corrected once before it shipped — a quotation on the essay this sheet follows is credited to the wrong book, and it is credited here to the right one.

Specimen On Being Ill Maker Virginia Woolf First printed The New Criterion, January 1926 This text The Hogarth Press, 1930 — revised by Woolf, and set in type by her Read 7 September 2026 Read by Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren Woolf wrote the essay about illness that English did not have, complained inside it that English could not hold one, and then went back four years later and quietly made her own sentences stranger. This sheet mounts the text as she left it in 1930.

records.heading: Illness has no place in literature
records.text: The essay opens with a list of what a temperature does to a person — the undiscovered countries, the wastes and deserts of the soul, the ancient and obdurate oaks uprooted by a bout of flu — and then lands on a complaint about the shelf: Specimen — the missing theme Novels devoted to influenza, she says; epic poems to typhoid; odes to pneumonia, lyrics to tooth-ache. It is a joke and it is not a joke. Love and battle and jealousy are the themes that got the canon, and every one of them is something a body does while upright and in motion. The condition that stops the body is the one the shelf has no room for. This is a claim about literature, and it is also a claim about who gets to be a subject. A century of Disabled and chronically ill writers have made the second claim directly. Woolf makes the first, in 1926, and leaves the second sitting underneath it.

quotes.text: …it becomes strange indeed that illness has not taken its place with love and battle and jealousy among the prime themes of literature.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.heading: The language runs dry
records.text: Her explanation for the gap is not squeamishness. It is vocabulary. Specimen — the poverty of the language It has all grown one way. A language is a record of what its speakers were required to be able to say. Hamlet got four centuries of vocabulary; the shiver got none. So the person in the bed is left, in Woolf's account, with nothing ready made — forced to coin words himself, and, taking his pain in one hand, and a lump of pure sound in the other… so to crush them together that a brand new word in the end drops out. She then does it herself. Chloral hydrate, the sedative she reaches for, arrives in the essay as that mighty Prince with the moths' eyes and the feathered feet, one of whose names is Chloral — a mythological figure invented on the spot because the pharmacological name will not carry what the drug means at four in the morning. Where we take this next is ours and not hers. Coining words for what the language has no room for is exactly what Autistic and Disabled communities have spent decades doing — monotropism, neuroqueer, bodymind, spoons. Woolf is describing one sufferer, one headache, and one doctor in the nineteen-twenties. She is not anticipating a lexicon that people would build a hundred years later out of their own lives. Reading her sentence forward to meet it is our move. The observation that the language grew one way is hers.

quotes.text: English, which can express the thoughts of Hamlet and the tragedy of Lear, has no words for the shiver and the headache. It has all grown one way.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.heading: Deserters
records.text: Then comes the sentence this sheet is named for. Woolf has been describing the effort health demands — the genial pretence, the endless obligation to communicate and share and work together — and the moment it stops: Specimen — the army of the upright Normativity, named as a posture. Not a belief, not an attitude — a way of holding the body that the rest of it is conscripted into. The army of the upright. Vertical, mobile, productive, on time. An inch of foot above the floor is enough to break the enlistment. What makes the sentence hold is that Woolf does not treat desertion as defeat. The deserter is the one who can finally look round, to look up—to look, for example, at the sky. The upright never see it: their sky is mutilated by chimneys and churches and serves as a background for man. Lying down is what gives it back. An essay that had only complained about being ill would not be on this site. This one says the position everyone is arranged into is a position, and that leaving it lets you see.

quotes.text: Directly the bed is called for, or, sunk deep among pillows in one chair, we raise our feet even an inch above the ground on another, we cease to be soldiers in the army of the upright; we become deserters. They march to battle.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.heading: The body intervenes
records.text: Underneath both arguments is a third, and it is the one that has aged least: Specimen — a sheet of plain glass The creature within, she writes, can only gaze through the pane — smudged or rosy — and cannot separate off from the body like the sheath of a knife or the pod of a pea for a single instant. That is a refusal of the mind–body split, written plainly, decades before the word bodymind was available to say it in one breath. Again: the word is not hers, and we are not putting it in her mouth. The refusal is.

quotes.text: …literature does its best to maintain that its concern is with the mind; that the body is a sheet of plain glass through which the soul looks straight and clear, and, save for one or two passions such as desire and greed, is null, and negligible and non-existent. On the contrary, the very opposite is true. All day, all night the body intervenes.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.heading: What this sheet will not tidy
records.text: The same essay is snobbish about the people doing the caring, and it reaches for empire when it wants a figure for effort. Sympathy, Woolf writes, is dispensed chiefly by the laggards and failures, women for the most part… who, having dropped out of the race, have time to spend upon fantastic and unprofitable excursions. She then names three of them by their initials, with real affection — the friend who builds up the nursery fender by the sickroom fire, the one who would ransack London for a giant tortoise to solace you. They are the reason the essay exists. They are also, in her sentence, the ones who lost. And the labour of staying upright is to communicate, to civilise, to share, to cultivate the desert, educate the native, to work together by day and by night to sport. The desert and the native are doing figurative work in a list about going to the office. That is the imperial imagination supplying a metaphor without being asked, in 1926, in a sentence about being tired. Neither of these is a reason to put the essay down, and neither gets softened here. An essay can see the arrangement of the upright with total clarity from inside the bed and still not see the arrangement of the sickroom it is lying in — who is paid, who is unpaid, who is a woman, who dropped out of a race she was never going to be allowed to win. Woolf is describing care work as the occupation of people with nothing better to do, while being kept alive by it. The sharpest reading of normativity in the essay is the one it does not turn on itself.

records.heading: She revised her own sentence
records.text: One more thing, and it is the reason this sheet names its edition on the label. On Being Ill exists in two states Woolf authorised. It appeared in The New Criterion in January 1926, and she revised it for the Hogarth Press edition of 1930 — two hundred and fifty signed copies, the type set by her. The revisions are not corrections. In the first paragraph alone: The first paragraph, 1926 and 1930 1926, The New Criterion 1930, The Hogarth Press brings to light brings to view uprooted in us in the act of sickness uprooted in us by the act of sickness when we think of this and infinitely more when we think of this with love, battle, and jealousy with love and battle and jealousy is null, negligible and non-existent is null, and negligible and non-existent Look at the last two. In 1926 those are lists, punctuated the way a list is supposed to be punctuated. In 1930 the commas open out into and…and…and, and the sentences stop being tidy. Love and battle and jealousy arrive one after another with no rest between them. Null, and negligible and non-existent piles up instead of resolving. It is the same move the essay is about. A writer who has just argued that the language grew one way went back into her own prose and un-grew it a little — in the direction of the breath, and away from the rule. She did it four years later, in type she set with her own hands, on a page she owned outright because the press was hers. So the edition is not a footnote here. Quote the 1926 commas and you are quoting Woolf. Quote the 1930 and…and…and and you are also quoting Woolf. Quote one and date it to the other and you have made a claim about her that is not true. This sheet reads 1930 because the revision is part of what it is reading. The 1926 text is scanned and online, and it is worth putting beside this one.

records.heading: In their indifference
records.text:
The essay ends up among flowers, because the deserter, flat on her back, has time to look at them properly. Woolf watches the sky first and finds it divinely beautiful… also divinely heartless — immeasurable resources spent on something with nothing to do with human profit. Then she looks down at the rose, which has been standing still and steady in the earth all afternoon while nobody watched. Specimen — the comfort Not that the flowers care. That they do not, and are therefore not asking anything of you. Nothing in that garden requires you to be upright, on time, or getting better. It is the one relation in the essay with no demand in it — and Woolf finds it, characteristically, at the exact moment she has stopped being able to stand up. Provenance
 Mounted 7 September 2026.
 Label corrected once, when Woolf’s two printings were read against each other ahead of the sheet;
 re-determined once, when the byline rule changed what kind of sheet this is.

quotes.text: It is in their indifference that they are comforting.
quotes.source: Virginia Woolf, On Being Ill, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

records.text: Specimen — the reading being read Octavia E. Butler gave Lauren Olamina a condition she calls hyperempathy: she feels the pain and the pleasure she sees in other people, in her own body, without being touched. Sami Schalk’s reading of the Parable novels is the best thing written about it, and it turns on one word — nonrealist. Hyperempathy, she argues, has no real-world equivalent, and that is precisely what stops a reader flattening it into a stereotype they already hold. Except that it does have one. Autistic people have been describing it for years, under the same name, and this sheet is about what happens to a careful argument when the thing it calls unreal turns out to be somebody’s Tuesday.

quotes.text: Bodymind is an essential concept in chapter 3 in my discussion of hyperempathy, a nonrealist disability that is both mental and physical in origin and manifestation.
quotes.source: Sami Schalk, Bodyminds Reimagined: (Dis)ability, Race, and Gender in Black Women’s Speculative Fiction, Duke University Press, 2018, Introduction, p. 5.

records.heading: What Butler built
records.text: Lauren says it plainly, early, and without any of the vocabulary that would later be built for it. Specimen — what she has The mechanism is perceptual, and Schalk is precise about it in a way most of her predecessors are not: what reaches Lauren is not another person’s feeling but her own reading of what she sees and hears. Specimen — the mechanism In the novel’s own world it has a cause and a chart entry. Lauren’s mother abused Paracetco, a designer smart pill, before Lauren was born; the doctors file the result as an organic delusional syndrome. It is hereditary from there. Lauren is emphatic that it is not a gift, not perception at a distance, not access to anybody’s interior: The sharing isn’t real, after all. It isn’t some magic or ESP that allows me to share the pain or the pleasure of other people. It’s delusional. Even I admit that. And she is equally emphatic that this changes nothing about what it does to her. Specimen — delusional or not Butler wrote the same thought again, six years later, at the top of the second novel, and put a harder edge on it. This is Lauren at twenty-three, dreaming her way back into a family whose pain no longer reaches her. Specimen — every damned bruise Even pains they pretended to feel, I did feel. That is the whole of the involuntariness in nine words, with the ordinary cruelty of brothers attached to it. And on the same page, three sentences that do a different kind of work: Specimen — the slack she was not cut They refused to let me be handicapped is held to the standard and denied the accommodation, in one sentence, delivered by the person it was done to and framed as a virtue of her upbringing. It is not offered as a grievance. That is what makes it recognisable.

quotes.text: I feel what I see others feeling or what I believe they feel.
quotes.source: Octavia E. Butler, Parable of the Sower, p. 12. Read in the Kindle edition, which is the copy every page reference on this sheet is keyed to.

quotes.text: On a basic level, hyperempathy is a congenital disability in which visual and auditory perceptions result in drastic sensations of pleasure or pain without any actual touch or contact with something or someone.
quotes.source: Sami Schalk, Bodyminds Reimagined, p. 89.

quotes.text: I get a lot of grief that doesn’t belong to me, and that isn’t real. But it hurts.
quotes.source: Octavia E. Butler, Parable of the Sower, p. 12.

quotes.text: Nevertheless I used to feel every damned bruise, cut, and burn that my brothers managed to collect. Each time I saw them hurt, I shared their pain as though I had been injured myself. Even pains they pretended to feel, I did feel. Hyperempathy syndrome is a delusional disorder, after all. There’s no telepathy, no magic, no deep spiritual awareness. There’s just the neurochemically-induced delusion that I feel the pain and pleasure that I see others experiencing. Pleasure is rare, pain is plentiful, and, delusional or not, it hurts like hell.
quotes.source: Octavia E. Butler, Parable of the Talents, p. 9. Not Sower — see the note at the foot of this sheet on how nearly it was filed there.

quotes.text: My father and stepmother cut me as little slack as possible when it came to my hyperempathy syndrome. They refused to let me be handicapped. I was the oldest kid, and that was that. I had my responsibilities.
quotes.source: Octavia E. Butler, Parable of the Talents, p. 9.

records.heading: The protection unfamiliarity buys
records.text: Schalk’s chapter opens by clearing the ground, and it is worth saying how much of it she clears. She identifies four totalizing readings of hyperempathy in the existing criticism — ignoring it, reading it as simply bad, reading it as a gift, and reading it as a metaphor for something else — and dismantles each. The gift readings are the ones she is hardest on, and she is right to be: they contradict what Lauren says about herself. She also names the pull behind them, and the phrase is exact. Specimen — the pull toward specialness Everything in the paragraph above is a debt this sheet owes her, and none of it is in dispute. The argument is with one move, and it is the move the chapter is built on. Specimen — the move This is a real and useful observation, and the chapter earns a great deal with it. A reader who has no prior category for hyperempathy cannot reach for one; they have to take Lauren’s account on Lauren’s terms, in context, which is exactly what Schalk wants and exactly what the four totalizing readings failed to do. And then she names the counter-example, in the same paragraph. The disability that is recognised, whose cultural familiarity does the damage she is describing, is autism — by way of Stuart Murray on sentimental narrative. Specimen — the cycle She is right about that too. But hold the two claims next to each other. Autism is the familiar thing that gets flattened; hyperempathy is the unfamiliar thing that cannot be. And the page turns straight into the sentence the rest of this sheet is a reply to. Specimen — unlike anything The chapter’s closing pages state it as a settled property of the object: this nonrealist disability resists the application of contemporary disability stereotypes and emphasizes the importance of context by having no real-world equivalent.

quotes.text: Representations of disability tend to provoke emotion, particularly pity or inspiration, and the positive readings of the Parable series may be influenced by a liberal compensatory desire to recast disability as “specialness,” to incorporate it without actually grappling with the challenges of inclusion or the negative aspects that can accompany some experiences of disability.
quotes.source: Sami Schalk, Bodyminds Reimagined, p. 92, on what she calls a subtle or passive ableism.

quotes.text: The nonrealist nature of hyperempathy, that is, the fact that it is not a disability we recognize in our current reality, disallows readers the ability to overlay preconceived notions about disabilities we recognize from our own world.
quotes.source: Sami Schalk, Bodyminds Reimagined, p. 95.
